questions.stem: "FIFO" means:
options: the last item added is the first one removed
the first item added is the first one removed
items are removed in sorted order
questions.explanation: Last in, first out (a) is a stack — Week 6.

questions.stem: enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), dequeue(), enqueue(4), dequeue(). What does the next dequeue() return?
questions.explanation: The queue goes [1, 2, 3] → dequeue 1 → [2, 3] → enqueue 4 → [2, 3, 4] → dequeue 2 → [3, 4]; the next dequeue returns 3. (A stack would have returned 4 — the difference in one question.)

questions.stem: In SlowQueue, dequeue is pop(0) on a DynamicArray. Its cost on a queue of n items is:
options: O(n) — every remaining element shifts one slot left
questions.explanation: pop(0) moves the n − 1 elements behind the front. Amortised O(1) (c) is the cost of append, the enqueue.

questions.stem: An array-based queue that enqueues with insert_at(0, x) and dequeues with pop() at the end has costs:
questions.explanation: pop() at the end moves nothing, but insert_at(0, x) shifts everything. With a plain array, whichever end is the front, one operation is O(n).

questions.stem: A CircularQueue with capacity 8 has head = 6 and size = 3. The next enqueue writes to slot:
questions.explanation: (6 + 3) % 8 = 9 % 8 = 1. Slot 9 (a) does not exist; the items are in slots 6, 7 and 0.

questions.stem: A CircularQueue with capacity 5 has head = 4 and size = 2. After one dequeue, head is:
questions.explanation: (4 + 1) % 5 = 0: the head wraps. Slot 5 (a) is past the end of the Array.

questions.stem: A ring buffer that stores only head and tail (no size) finds head == tail. The queue is:
options: either full or empty — it cannot tell which
questions.explanation: Empty: nothing between head and tail. Full: the tail has come all the way round to the head. Both look the same.

questions.stem: CircularQueue keeps a _size field because:
options: it tells a full ring from an empty one, which look the same by head and tail
len would otherwise be O(n) with no other benefit
the Array does not know its own length
questions.explanation: With the size, empty is size == 0 and full is size == capacity. The Array does know its length (c): len(block).

questions.stem: A full ring of capacity 4 holds [E, F, C, D] with head = 2. It grows to capacity 8 by copying new[i] = old[i] and keeping head = 2. Read front to back, the queue is now:
questions.explanation: Slots 2 and 3 of the new block hold C and D, slots 4 and 5 are empty, and E and F sit in slots 0 and 1 — behind the front. The correct copy gives (a) with head = 0.

questions.stem: A queue on a singly linked list with head and tail references should put the front of the queue at:
options: either end — it makes no difference
questions.explanation: Dequeue at the head (pop_front, O(1)), enqueue after the tail (O(1)).

questions.stem: Why not dequeue at the tail of a singly linked list?
options: Removing the last node needs the node before it, which takes an O(n) walk
The tail node has no value
It would make the queue LIFO
questions.explanation: The new tail is the node before the old one, and a singly linked list can only find it by walking from the head.

questions.stem: A queue built from two stacks (inbox and outbox, pouring only when outbox is empty): enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), dequeue(). How many items are now in outbox?
questions.explanation: The first dequeue finds outbox empty and pours all three: outbox holds 3, 2, 1 (1 on top). It pops 1, leaving 2 and 3.

questions.stem: The cost of dequeue on that two-stack queue is:
options: amortised O(1) — each item is poured from inbox to outbox at most once
questions.explanation: One dequeue can pour n items, so the worst case (c) is O(n), but each item is pushed, poured and popped once in its life.

questions.stem: Which of these needs a queue?
questions.explanation: BFS visits nodes in the order they were discovered: FIFO. The other three are stack applications from Week 6.

questions.stem: n enqueues followed by n dequeues on a SlowQueue cost in total:
questions.explanation: Dequeue number i shifts n − i elements: (n-1) + (n-2) + … + 0 = n(n-1)/2.

questions.stem: In Python, (0 - 1) % 8 is:
questions.explanation: Python's % takes the sign of the divisor, so the result is in 0..7: stepping back from slot 0 wraps to slot 7. In C or Java the answer would be −1 (a).

questions.stem: A deque is a structure that:
options: serves the most urgent item first
can only be used as a stack
adds and removes at both ends
questions.explanation: A double-ended queue. (a) is a priority queue.

questions.stem: Measured, a ring-buffer dequeue and a linked-queue dequeue are both flat lines as n grows, but the ring is about five times slower. The reason:
options: a constant factor: the % and the bounds-checked Array access on every operation
the ring is really O(log n)
the ring copies the queue on every dequeue
the linked queue is O(1) and the ring is O(n)
questions.explanation: Both are O(1); the ring pays more per operation. Big-O hides constant factors, and measurement shows them.

questions.stem: Five people A, B, C, D, E stand in a circle; counting from A, every second person leaves. Who is left last?
questions.explanation: B, D, A and E leave in that order (W7-C2); C is last.

questions.stem: An array queue with a head index but no wrap-around, 8 slots: 8 enqueues, then 5 dequeues. How many more enqueues fit without growing the block?
questions.explanation: Tail = 8: there is no slot 8, even though slots 0 to 4 are dead and free. That is why the queue must wrap.

questions.stem: A CircularQueue that doubles its capacity when full has an enqueue cost of:
questions.explanation: The occasional copy is O(n), but doubling makes the copies total less than 2n over n enqueues — Lecture 04's argument.

questions.stem: A priority queue (Week 12) differs from a queue because it dequeues:
options: the most urgent item, not the oldest
questions.explanation: Same two operations, a different rule — and a different structure underneath, the heap.

questions.stem: A CircularQueue(4), starting empty: enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), enqueue(4), dequeue(), dequeue(), enqueue(5). Which describes the ring now?
options: head = 0, size = 3, and 5 is in slot 0
head = 2, size = 3, and 5 is in slot 4
head = 2, size = 3, and 5 is in slot 0
head = 2, size = 4, and 5 is in slot 1
questions.explanation: After four enqueues the ring is full (1 2 3 4, head 0). Two dequeues move head to 2, size 2. The tail is (2 + 2) % 4 = 0, so 5 goes into slot 0, freed by 1. Slot 4 (b) does not exist: that is the missing %. Head 0 (a) forgets that dequeue moves the head; size 4 (d) counts the dequeued items.

questions.stem: A CircularQueue(5), starting empty: enqueue A, B, C, D, E; dequeue three times; enqueue F, then G. What is in the block, from slot 0 to slot 4?
options: None None None D E F G
questions.explanation: The three dequeues leave D, E in slots 3 and 4, with head 3. F goes to (3 + 2) % 5 = 0, G to slot 1, and slot 2 is still empty. (b) is list(q), the queue order, not the block. (d) forgets that dequeue clears the slot it read, so C is gone. (c) has seven slots in a five-slot block.

questions.stem: A full CircularQueue of capacity 4 holds C D E F (front to back), with head = 2. enqueue(G) makes the correct _grow double the block first. Afterwards, head is ___ and G is in slot ___:
questions.explanation: _grow copies in queue order: C D E F go to slots 0–3 and head becomes 0. Then G is written at (0 + 4) % 8 = 4. (a) is what happens if head is kept, which is the naive grow of W7-M09. (b) would overwrite the front.

questions.stem: A student's _grow copies in queue order into an Array(8) and sets head = 0, but forgets to set self._capacity = 8. On the full ring of W7-M25, enqueue(G) then:
options: works, because the new block really has 8 slots
writes G to slot (0 + 4) % 4 = 0, over the front item C
raises IndexError, because slot 4 is out of range
writes G to slot 4, but len(q) stays 4
questions.explanation: The tail is still computed modulo 4: (0 + 4) % 4 = 0, so G overwrites C, the front, and list(q) reads G D E F G. No error is raised, which is what makes the bug dangerous: (c) is wrong. (a) is wrong because the arithmetic, not the block, decides where G goes.

questions.stem: A dequeue updates the head with self._head += 1 instead of self._head = (self._head + 1) % self._capacity. On a CircularQueue(4): enqueue A, B, C, D; dequeue four times; enqueue E; dequeue. What happens?
options: The first dequeue fails: head starts beyond the block
Every operation works; the last dequeue returns E
The last dequeue raises IndexError: it reads slot 4 of a 4-slot block
questions.explanation: The four dequeues read slots 0–3, so they work, and head ends at 4. The enqueue writes E at (4 + 0) % 4 = 0, which also works. Then the dequeue reads self._block[4], and the Array raises IndexError. The bug hides until the head has gone once round the ring: (b) is what the correct code does.

questions.stem: A linked queue's enqueue tests if self._tail is None: to decide that the queue is empty, and its dequeue moves head on but never resets tail. After enqueue(1), dequeue(), enqueue(2), the next dequeue():
options: raises IndexError: 2 was linked after the old, removed node, and head is still None
questions.explanation: After the first dequeue, head is None but tail still refers to the removed node 1. So enqueue(2) takes the else branch and links 2 after that dead node, and head stays None. The next dequeue finds head None and raises, although len says 1. The fix: when the queue becomes empty, reset tail to None too (W7-B4).

questions.stem: A queue from two stacks (pour only when outbox is empty). Count every push and pop on the two stacks, including the pours: enqueue 1, 2, 3; dequeue; enqueue 4, 5; dequeue three times. How many stack operations is that in total?
questions.explanation: Each item costs at most four operations: push to inbox, pop from inbox, push to outbox, pop from outbox. Items 1–4 are dequeued, so 4 × 4 = 16. Item 5 was poured but not dequeued, so 3 more: 19. Step by step: 3 pushes; a pour of 3 items (6) and 1 pop; 2 pushes; 2 pops; a pour of 2 (4) and 1 pop. (b) and (a) forget to count the pours as two operations per item; (c) is not a real count.

questions.stem: A ring buffer that leaves one slot unused to tell full from empty has a block of 8 slots. It holds at most:
questions.explanation: One slot always stays empty, so that head == tail can only mean empty. Eight slots hold seven items. (a) would need a size field, which is what dsa/queue.py keeps.

questions.stem: A ring with 8 slots stores only head and tail and leaves one slot unused. Now head = 3 and tail = 2. How many items does it hold, and is it full?
options: 0 items: head and tail are next to each other, so it is empty
questions.explanation: The size is (tail - head) % 8 = (2 - 3) % 8 = 7, and full is defined as (tail + 1) % 8 == head: 3 == 3. With one slot left unused, 7 is the most an 8-slot ring can hold, so (d) is impossible. (a) reads the distance the wrong way round; (b) confuses tail + 1 == head (full) with head == tail (empty).

questions.stem: CircularQueue.dequeue sets the slot it read back to None. Why?
options: is_empty checks for None in the head slot
so the block no longer refers to the dequeued object, which can then be freed
enqueue looks for a None slot to write into
without it, __iter__ would show the dequeued value
questions.explanation: The slot is outside the live part of the ring, so the queue is correct without clearing it (a, c and d are wrong: is_empty uses _size, enqueue uses (head + size) % capacity, and __iter__ walks only size slots from head). But the block would keep a reference to the object, and Python's garbage collector could not free it.

questions.stem: Which of these is a typical use of a ring buffer?
options: the undo history of an editor
keeping the last 1,000 lines of a log, overwriting the oldest
questions.explanation: A fixed block that overwrites its oldest entry is exactly a ring buffer. Brackets (a) and undo (b) need stacks; sorting (c) needs neither.

questions.stem:
What does this print?

q = CircularQueue()
q.enqueue("1")
for _ in range(6):
    s = q.dequeue()
    print(s, end=" ")
    q.enqueue(s + "0")
    q.enqueue(s + "1")
questions.explanation: The queue gives breadth-first order: the children of 1 (10, 11) are dequeued before the children of 10 (100, 101), and those before the children of 11 (110, 111). That is the binary numbers 1 to 6, in order. (b) follows one branch only (depth-first); (d) swaps 100 and 101; (c) enqueues s + "1" first.

questions.stem: Six people, 1 to 6, are put in a queue. Until one is left: move two people from the front to the back, then dequeue the third, who leaves. In what order do they leave, and who is left?
questions.explanation: Queue 1 2 3 4 5 6: move 1, 2, remove 3. Queue 4 5 6 1 2: move 4, 5, remove 6. Queue 1 2 4 5: move 1, 2, remove 4. Queue 5 1 2: move 5, 1, remove 2. Queue 5 1: move 5, 1, remove 5. 1 is left. (a) removes 2 before 4: it loses track after the queue wraps.

questions.stem: A graph search dequeues a node, then enqueues its unvisited neighbours, and repeats. If the queue is replaced by a stack (pop instead of dequeue, push instead of enqueue), the same loop:
questions.explanation: The stack hands back the most recently found node first, so the search goes as deep as it can before backing up. That is why Week 14 puts bfs and dfs_iterative side by side: the loops are the same, and only the structure differs. (c) cannot happen as long as visited nodes are not added again.

questions.stem: With Python's collections.deque, the O(1) way to remove the front item of a queue d is:
questions.explanation: popleft() removes the front in O(1). deque.pop() (b) removes the back, and deque.pop(0) (a) is an error: pop takes no argument. On a list, pop(0) would work but costs O(n). deque has no dequeue method (c).

questions.stem: A moving average of the last k readings keeps a CircularQueue(k) and a running total beside it. The running total is there because:
options: it tells a full window from an empty one
each new average then costs O(1), instead of O(k) to add up the window again
floating-point sums are only exact that way
questions.explanation: When a reading arrives, subtract the value that leaves the window and add the new one: O(1) per update. Adding up k values each time would cost O(k). The ring can be iterated (a), and _size tells full from empty (b).

questions.stem: A CircularQueue with capacity 6 has head = 4 and size = 5. Front to back, the queue's items are in slots:
questions.explanation: Slot of offset i is (4 + i) % 6, for i = 0 to 4: 4, 5, then round to 0, 1, 2. (b) forgets the %; (c) ignores head; (d) walks backwards.

questions.stem: A naive _grow copies new[i] = old[i] and keeps head. It passes a test that fills a fresh CircularQueue(4) with A, B, C, D and then enqueues E. Why does the test not catch the bug?
options: The naive copy is in fact correct
The ring has not wrapped: head is 0, so slot order and queue order are the same
Array reorders its slots when it grows
questions.explanation: With head = 0, the i-th item of the queue really is in slot i, so copying slot by slot happens to give the right order. The naive copy goes wrong only once the data has wrapped: on the ring of W7-M25 it gives C D None None G. So (a) is wrong. A test must wrap the ring before it grows it.

essays.stem: State the Queue ADT with the cost of each operation. Explain why an array-based queue that shifts is O(n) per dequeue, and why swapping which end is the front does not help. How does a ring buffer fix it?
essays.answer:
• ADT: enqueue(x) at the back, dequeue() from the front (FIFO), is_empty, len — all O(1); dequeue raises IndexError when empty.
  • Shifting: on a plain array the front is a fixed position, index 0; removing it moves the n − 1 others: O(n).
  • Swapping ends does not help: the back at index 0 makes enqueue shift everything instead. A queue uses both ends, and an array is cheap at only one.
  • Ring buffer: do not move data, move the indices. head marks the front; the back is (head + size) % capacity; both wrap round with %, so slots freed at the front are reused. Every operation O(1).

essays.stem: In a ring buffer, head == tail can mean two different things. Explain which two, with an example of each, and describe two ways of telling them apart. Which one does dsa/queue.py use?
essays.answer:
• Empty: nothing in the ring, e.g. a new queue: head = tail = 0.
  • Full: the tail has caught up with the head, e.g. capacity 4, head 2, four items: tail = (2 + 4) % 4 = 2.
  • Fixes: (1) keep a count size — empty is size == 0, full is size == capacity; (2) leave one slot always unused — full is (tail + 1) % capacity == head, so head == tail means only empty; (3) a flag set when an enqueue makes head equal tail.
  • dsa/queue.py keeps _size (and computes the tail from it).

essays.stem: A full CircularQueue must grow. Explain, with an example, why copying the block slot by slot gives a wrong queue once the data has wrapped, give the correct copy, and explain why doubling keeps enqueue amortised O(1).
essays.answer:
• Example: capacity 4, head 2, block [E, F, C, D], queue C D E F. A slot-by-slot copy into 8 slots keeps C, D in slots 2, 3 and E, F in slots 0, 1; with head 2 the queue now reads C, D, then empty slots — E and F are lost behind the front.
  • Correct copy: in queue order: new[i] = old[(head + i) % old_capacity] for i in 0..size − 1, then head = 0 (and the capacity updated).
  • Amortised O(1): a copy happens only when the ring is full, and doubling means the copies after n enqueues total 1 + 2 + 4 + … < 2n: O(n) over n operations, O(1) each on average.
  • It only goes wrong once the data has wrapped, which is why it survives tests that never dequeue before growing.

essays.stem: Describe a queue built from two stacks. Show that it is amortised O(1) per operation, and explain why pouring must happen only when the outbox is empty.
essays.answer:
• inbox takes every enqueue; dequeue pops outbox, and when outbox is empty it first pours all of inbox into it — which reverses them, so the oldest is on top.
  • Amortised: each item is pushed on inbox once, moved to outbox once and popped once — three O(1) steps in its life, so n operations cost O(n).
  • Pour only when empty: pouring into a non-empty outbox would put newer items on top of older ones and break FIFO; pouring back and forth on every dequeue keeps FIFO but costs O(n) per dequeue (W7-K3).

essays.stem: Compare the ring buffer and the linked queue (with head and tail): cost per operation, memory, and when you would choose each. Where does Python's collections.deque fit?
essays.answer:
• Ring buffer: O(1) (amortised if it grows); one contiguous block, no allocation per item, good locality. Choose it when the maximum size is known or bounded — hardware and OS buffers — or for speed in general.
  • Linked queue: O(1) worst case, never copies; but a node per item (more memory, scattered). Choose it when a worst-case guarantee matters more than memory.
  • collections.deque combines them: a doubly linked list of fixed blocks — O(1) at both ends, few allocations. It is what to use in real Python code.

essays.stem: Three ring-buffer bugs: the tail computed as head + size with no %; the head moved with head += 1 with no %; and a _grow that never updates _capacity. For each, say what goes wrong and the shortest operation sequence that shows it. Why do all three pass a test that never wraps the ring?
essays.answer:
• No % on the tail: once the back reaches the end of the block, the write goes to slot capacity and the Array raises IndexError, although there are free slots at the front. Shortest: CircularQueue(2): enqueue, enqueue, dequeue, enqueue (tail = 1 + 1 = 2).
  • No % on the head: dequeues work until head reaches capacity; the next dequeue reads slot capacity and raises. Shortest: CircularQueue(1): enqueue, dequeue (head = 1), enqueue (written to (1 + 0) % 1 = 0), dequeue.
  • _capacity not updated in _grow: the new block is bigger, but every % still wraps at the old size, so the next enqueue after the grow overwrites the front, silently. Shortest: fill a ring of capacity 1, enqueue twice more.
  • Why the tests miss them: while the ring has not wrapped, head is 0 and head + size is below the capacity, so % changes nothing. Every test must take the ring round at least once, and grow it after it has wrapped.

essays.stem: When a ring buffer is full, it can refuse (a bounded queue) or grow. Explain both choices, give a real use for each, and say which level_order and bfs need, and why.
essays.answer:
• Refuse (bounded): raise an error, or make the producer wait, or drop data when full. Memory is fixed. Used for audio and network buffers, and keyboard buffers, where memory must not grow.
  • Grow: allocate a block twice as big and copy in queue order; enqueue stays amortised O(1). Used for general-purpose queues such as collections.deque.
  • level_order and bfs need a growing queue: they cannot know in advance how many nodes will be waiting at once (a whole level of a tree, a whole frontier of a graph), and refusing would make the search fail.

essays.stem: Describe enqueue and dequeue for a queue on a singly linked list with head and tail, including the empty cases. Explain why the front must be the head, and what goes wrong if dequeue does not reset tail when the queue becomes empty.
essays.answer:
• enqueue: make a node. If the queue is empty, it becomes both head and tail; otherwise set tail.next to it and move tail to it. O(1).
  • dequeue: IndexError if empty; otherwise take head.value, move head to head.next; if head is now None, set tail = None too. O(1).
  • Front at the head: removing at the head is O(1); removing the last node of a singly linked list needs the node before it, an O(n) walk. So we add at the tail and remove at the head.
  • Stale tail: tail still refers to the removed node. If enqueue tests tail to detect emptiness, the new node is linked after that dead node and head stays None: len says 1, but the next dequeue raises. (If it tests head, the bug hides, but tail still keeps a dead node alive.)

essays.stem: Explain why breadth-first order needs a queue, using the binary numbers 1, 10, 11, 100, … generated from "1" (dequeue s, enqueue s + "0" and s + "1"). What order do you get if the queue is replaced by a stack, and why?
essays.answer:
• A queue hands items back in the order they were discovered: everything at one level is dequeued before anything at the next. From "1": dequeue 1, enqueue 10, 11; dequeue 10, enqueue 100, 101; dequeue 11, enqueue 110, 111…
  • So the order is 1, 10, 11, 100, 101, 110, 111, …: the binary numbers in increasing order, level by level (by length).
  • With a stack, the last item found comes out first: 1, 11, 111, 1111, … (with s + "0" pushed before s + "1"). The search goes deep along one branch and never comes back to 10. That is depth-first order, as in Week 14.
